title: VC0-03205
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants), citizens of Nigeria, appeal the negative decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated September 18, 2020.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellants), citizens of Nigeria, appeal the negative decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated September 18, 2020.
The Appellants were joined in their claims for protection at the RPD with their mother, XXXX XXXX XXXX, who was the Principal Claimant and remains their Designated Representative (DR).

The Appellants' mother's claim for protection was accepted on September 18, 2020, based on her membership in a particular social group, a bisexual Nigerian woman who had been arrested by the police for engaging in illegal LGBTQ activities. The claim for protection for the minor claimants was denied. Originally, the Appellants came to Canada with their mother and father; however, just prior to the planned vacation in Canada, the Appellants' mother had been arrested and accused of engaging in LGBTQ activities. Her husband was unaware of her circumstances as her girlfriend had bribed and secured her release from custody. Once in Canada, the Appellants' father learned of his wife's bisexual activities and romantic involvement with a woman and left her and the children and returned to Nigeria. He threatened to expose the Appellants' mother to the community and the family, so that upon her return, she would be punished.

The Appellants' mother was found credible in establishing her LGBTQ identity, and her claim for protection was accepted. The minor claimants were found not to be Convention refugees, nor persons in need of protection, as the RPD concluded that they did not face any risk on return to Nigeria, based upon membership in a particular social group, the children of an LGBTQ parent.

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred as there is objective evidence supporting the risk to the minor Appellants based on their mother's sexual orientation. They ask that I allow the appeal and find the Appellants to be Convention refugees, or in the alternative, I allow the appeal and remit the matter back to the RPD for consideration before a differently constituted panel.1

After a review of the record on the standard of correctness,2 I find that the RPD did not err and find that the Appellants have not established a forward-looking risk objectively. The appeals are dismissed. NEW EVIDENCE The evidence presented by the Appellants is rejected

According to the law,3 I can only accept evidence that: i. arose after the RPD decision; or ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.4

The Appellant seek to admit objective evidence found in the National Documentation Package (NDP); however, the Memorandum does not reference a specific date for the NDP.5 I note that the referenced Item 6.11 is contained in the NDP for both July 31, 20206 and the more recent NDP, for November 30, 2020,7 at the same item number. Therefore, this evidence was before the panel at the RPD hearing and is not new.
As the Appellants have not explained how this evidence is new, and I confirm that it is not new by its date, it is not admissible as new evidence. Therefore no oral hearing is granted.
The Chairperson's Guidelines on Child Refugee Claimants have been considered in this decision.

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred with the following two key findings: * The Appellants do not have a well-founded fear because they were never targeted in the past; * There is no objective evidence in the NDP to support a risk to family members of LGBTQ individuals.

The Appellants are correct in stating that one does not need to establish past persecution to be successful with a refugee claim. It is the forward-looking risk8 that leads to a well-founded claim. By definition, a Convention refugee is someone who has a well-founded fear of persecution, both subjectively and objectively.9

The RPD found the Appellants' mother credible regarding the establishment of her bisexual orientation; as such, I am bound by the positive credibility finding of the RPD on the evidence provided by the Appellants' mother on identity. She testified that she feared that her children would face community persecution and that family members may poison the children against her due to her bisexuality. She also feared that her children would be stoned.10

While the RPD found the Appellants' mother credible with the establishment of her profile, it also found that the Appellants' mother had failed to adduce sufficient credible evidence of a future risk to her children from her husband or other family members.11

The Appellants' mother indicated that her husband had been violent in the past; however, my review of the record indicates that there were no questions on this issue by her counsel. In addition, no new evidence has been provided to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) as an update on the situation with family members in Nigeria, or in support of these allegations of any risk to the Appellants in Nigeria from their father or other family members. Overall, there is insufficient evidence on the record establishing that the Appellants have a profile as victims of family violence. In fact, the Appellants' mother also testified that her husband is not interested in custody of the children, which is reflected in his departure from Canada without asserting his rights to custody.12

In this appeal, the Appellants submit that the RPD erred when they overlooked the impact of stigmatization and ostracization of the minor Appellants in their community due to their mother's sexual orientation. They argue that the RPD failed to consider the objective evidence in its entirety. While the RPD did quote objective materials,13 the Appellants argue that they ignored other parts of the objective materials.

I agree that the RPD should have indicated consideration of the materials specific to children, as the more relevant the evidence is, the more likely there is to be an error in omitting it;14 however, after considering the objective evidence and the Appellants' submission, I come to the same conclusion as the RPD.

While it is agreed that the objective evidence speaks to discrimination against LGBTQ individuals, in areas of housing, health care and employment, as well as police mistreatment,15 it also indicates that the experiences of community discrimination and hate crimes against LGBTQ community members in Nigeria is tempered by social status and social class.16

Specific to the situation of these Appellants, however, it is noted in the objective material that children may experience discrimination, neglect or stigma as a child of a sexual minority who is left behind.17 The same objective evidence also reports: ...when the person who is a sexual minority is no longer in Nigeria, the family members do not face any risks from society or authorities, "[e]xcept in a situation where the family is popular and very public with their support of their child" who is a sexual minority....the stigma and shame that family members of sexual minorities face is "considerably reduced" once the person who is a sexual minority is no longer in Nigeria.18 [citations omitted]

As the Appellants' mother is in Canada and can remain, there is insufficient objective evidence establishing that the Appellants will face persecution on return as children of an LGBTQ mother residing in Canada. The Appellants have not provided any new objective evidence supporting a risk either.

The Appellants have not established a profile with sufficient evidence which gives rise, objectively, to a serious possibility of persecution on return to Nigeria. If the Appellants face a risk of stoning as their mother alleged at the RPD hearing, it would be reasonable to see it widely reported in the objective evidence before the RAD. The numerous pieces of objective evidence contained in the NDP for Nigeria is collected from a wide variety of disinterested third-party sources including non-governmental organizations (NGOs) involved in LGBTQ advocacy.
As a result, I agree with the RPD conclusion that the claims of the minor children are not well founded objectively.

I dismiss the appeals and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
